Except for the aforementioned seismic typology, few studies have
attempted to account for rockfall trajectory and mass estimation using
seismic analysis, which are crucial issues for emergency response and
rockfall assessment. Feng et al. (2021) utilized the time difference of the
rockfall signal from each station to locate every roll/bounce point.
However, a complex geological background with path and site effects
influences transmission velocity and recorded amplitudes of seismic
signals, presenting inconsistent performances in determining the source
location. Furthermore, the station distribution from the research was
only located on the upslope area, and rocks moved downslope. The poor
station coverage of the rockfall trajectory may affect the location per-
formance. Thus, locating bounce and falling points on the ground is still
an unsolved problem in rockfall monitoring. In addition to the time-
based method (TB) for source location, the amplitude-based method
(ASL), which has not yet been applied in a location of slope scale
rockfall, is another practical way to determine the source location
(Walsh et al., 2017). Here, we then discuss their pros and cons, offering a
method for reliable location results. This method suggests a strategy of
station distribution for rockfall monitoring in advance. Moreover, for
the rock mass issue, Hibert et al. (2017) adopted a single boulder
experiment and indicated that the seismic signal amplitude correlates to
the rock's momentum. Nevertheless, obtaining information about the
velocity of moving rock in actual rockfall events is lacking. Additional
parameters need to be taken into account for practical application.
Huang et al. (2007) found that the size of the boulder relates to the
extension of the seismic signal towards the low-frequency band, a
feature that could be a potential tool for rock mass estimation. We have
included this concept in this study.

4.6. Future perspective
To enhance the generalizability of our research findings, several
prerequisites and procedures must be taken into account to apply
seismic techniques for source location, rockfall tracking, and mass
estimation to other slopes (Fig. 10). Firstly, in terms of location, we
suggest conducting drone surveys to generate digital elevation models,
using a sledgehammer to clarify the path effects, and analyzing earth-
quake signals to correct site-specific effects. In adapting ASL and TB, site
and path effects should also be considered, respectively. Ultimately, a
reliable location for initial rock-ground impact is achieved by identi-
fying the overlapping area of both results with high relative fitness
. Secondly, avoiding frequency bands saturated with ambient
noise for rockfall tracking by seismic energy ratio is essential. Con-
ducting HR and LR can help to identify the feature of the rock mass
approaching/departing from a station and the timing of rock-ground
impacts. Finally, the lowest frequency during the rockfall process and
rock mass can be used in repeated experiments to build an empirical
regression for future applications in the experimental site.
